item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers right-handed pitcher Emmet Sheehan sent a message to the team ahead of the postseason with his role on the team still uncertain.
Sheehan went to the minors at the beginning of August following the arrival of Tarik Skubal and a string of poor results on his part. Prior to his stint in the minors, Sheehan had a 5.29 ERA and had just allowed five earned runs in just 2.2 innings pitched.
How Long Was Emmet Sheehan in the Minors?
He managed to get right in the minors, though, allowing just three earned runs over the course of 18 innings pitched in Triple-A. He returned in the middle of September, and has three starts under his belt since returning.
In those appearances, Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA over the course of 17 innings pitched, striking out 24 batters. He pitched Sunday, striking out nine batters through 5.1 scoreless innings of relief, during which he only allowed one hit and one walk. On the year, Sheehan now has a 4.57 ERA through 112.1 innings pitched, striking out 132 batters during his time in MLB.
The Dodgers are optioning him back to Triple-A to keep their bullpen fresh throughout the remainder of the season as they look to secure the No. 2 seed in the NL, but he can still feature in the postseason and is willing to do whatever it takes to help the team.
“I feel like I’m in a much better spot now,” Sheehan told Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez and reporters. “Whatever role they want me to do going forward, I’m ready to do it. It was nice to get that experience coming out of the pen, and I’m ready to go.”
What Role Would Emmet Sheehan Have in the Postseason?
Sheehan has predominantly played as a starter for the Dodgers this season, making his first relief appearance of the year on Sunday, but would almost definitely stay in the bullpen if he makes the roster come October.
The Dodgers have a four-man rotation planned out already, as Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Skubal are all healthy and likely to be the Dodgers’ starters during the postseason.
Sheehan would fit in the bullpen as a long relief arm, and would likely be the Dodgers’ go-to man in those scenarios.
Landon Knack and Bobby Miller have taken on those responsibilities as of late, but Sheehan’s recent results should qualify him for a spot over both Knack and Miller.
Will the Dodgers Bring Emmet Sheehan to the Postseason?
The Dodgers are allowed a maximum of 13 pitchers on their roster for the postseason, and Sheehan will almost certainly be included in those options due to his ability to pitch out of the bullpen.
Sheehan came out of the bullpen for the Dodgers during last year’s postseason, and while he wasn’t the most effective in that role, his recent surge and experience in that area will be key for LA as they look to win a third consecutive World Series.
The right-hander won’t pitch again for the Dodgers in the regular season due to the minimum 15-day stay in the minors, so unless the Dodgers need to recall him due to an injury, he’ll hope the impression he made during his strong September is enough to warrant a spot on the postseason roster.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star pitcher Tyler Glasnow shut down any injury concerns on Friday after a scare last week.
Glasnow looked like his usual self against the San Francisco Giants. He allowed only two runs on three hits and two walks while striking out 10 over six innings to earn his fifth win of the season.
Dodgers skipper Dave Roberts couldn't be more pleased with his outing and, more importantly, loves to see Glasnow healthy heading into the postseason.
“It is just making sure he’s feeling good, he’s healthy, which he is,” Roberts said. “So now it’s just letting him go do what he does and bet on the talent to perform. That’s where I think we all feel good, especially Tyler right now, just knowing the health and where the head’s at, all that stuff. We’re in a good spot.”
Roberts' tone on Friday was different than Glasnow's last outing on Sunday against Miami.
“He’s a big-bodied guy, so there’s a lot of big moving parts,” Roberts said last Sunday. “So sometimes if they get out of whack a little bit, it’s hard to just sync everything up.”
Last week, Glasnow's outing was concerning. Not only did he get the loss against the Miami Marlins, but the 33-year-old was also far from himself.
Roberts said he "didn't feel great" after the fact.
Nonetheless, Glasnow noted that there was nothing to be worried about.
“It wasn’t anything crazy,” Glasnow said. “But I definitely feel better now than I did then."
“Right now, I feel pretty good,” he added. “We worked on some stuff after that last start. Just tried to keep for this start, take it in the next start. And then hopefully everything is feeling good for playoffs.”
Tyler Glasnow Looking to Round Into Form Before Postseason
Glasnow's outing on Friday was his fifth since returning from the 60-day IL.
The 33-year-old dealt with a back injury that held him to seven starts. Before his return in late August, Glasnow last pitched in early May.
Overall, Glasnow has tallied a 3.46 ERA, 87 strikeouts and a 0.96 WHIP in 67.2 innings this season. He'll be relied upon heavily come October as the team's fourth starter.
Glasnow is in his third season in Los Angeles after the Dodgers traded for him in December 2023. In that time, Glasnow has landed on the injured list multiple times but has been stellar when healthy.
In 52 games, Glasnow has a 18-10 record, 361 strikeouts, a 3.39 ERA and a 0.99 WHIP in 292 innings.
He made six appearances (three starts) in last year's postseason, sporting a 1.69 ERA across 21.1 innings with 25 strikeouts. He earned the save in Game 6 of the World Series and took down seven outs in Game 7.

item.content:encoded:
Entering the final week of the regular season, the Dodgers more or less know their postseason fate.
They've locked up the National League West. They are a seemingly safe four games clear of the Atlanta Braves for a first-round bye. And, unless they can close a two-game gap on the Milwaukee Brewers without holding the tiebreaker, they will finish as the NL's No. 2 seed, getting home-field advantage at least for the NL Division Series.
Thus, the real intrigue for now is who might be on the Dodgers' postseason roster when the playoffs begin next month.
This year, injuries and fluctuating performances have forced them to cycle 53 different players through their clubhouse.
And while the core of the group is clear, many questions remain about how the club will construct its lineup and pitching staff for this fall's pursuit of a third-straight World Series.
Here is the California Post's best guess about how it will all shake out.
Lineup locks
Will Smith, Freddie Freeman, Tommy Edman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy, Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia
There won't be any big surprises in how the Dodgers line up to begin the playoffs, assuming Ohtani is healthy enough to resume everyday DH'ing duties.
Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker have cemented their place as everyday hitters thanks to late-season surges. Andy Pages is due back on Tuesday from a fractured hand. Freddie Freeman still seems somewhat limited by his right knee injury, but has nonetheless been able to manage it well enough to this point. And while Tommy Edman has been slumping lately, he doesn't seem to be in immediate danger of losing at-bats.
On the bench, Hunter Feduccia has locked up the back-up catching job, and could be a left-handed hitting option as a pinch-hitter. Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, meanwhile, each provide versatile defensive depth, as well as extensive track records for postseason heroics when called upon.
Entering the final week of the regular season, the core of the Dodgers' position player group looks as they expected.
Dodgers Lineup questions
Bubble candidates: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, Alex Freeland, Hyeseong Kim
The Dodgers will still have one, if not two, position player spots to fill depending on how they construct their roster (i.e. an even 13 pitchers/13 hitters, or a 12/14 split like they used last year?)
And for those, they could have a number of difficult decisions.
First and foremost: Will Josue De Paula make the playoff roster?
If he does, it will likely be as a left-handed bench bat; though if there is any lingering uncertainty with Ohtani, he could also provide insurance as a backup DH option. His main competition right now figures to be Alex Call (who might be redundant to Rojas and Hernández as a right-handed bench bat) or Dalton Rushing (who is an intriguing alternative as a left-handed bat, but remains sidelined from the setback he suffered with his elbow injury earlier this month).
In just 10 MLB games, De Paula has quickly built a strong case, showing supreme plate discipline (10 walks to only four strikeouts) and the potential for power (three doubles, one home run, seven RBIs). At this point, it might be more of a surprise if he doesn't make it.
If the Dodgers elect to carry an extra position player on top of that, the choices are even more varied.
Last year, they rostered two base-running/defensive specialists throughout the playoffs in infielder Hyeseong Kim and outfielder Justin Dean. Dean is now gone, and Hernández could serve as a late-game defensive outfield replacement anyway. But Kim remains in consideration, manager Dave Roberts said, thanks to his speed and infield glove. Alex Freeland could also factor in here, as someone capable of providing more at the plate.
Lineup projection for Los Angeles
C: Will Smith
1B: Freddie Freeman
2B: Tommy Edman
SS: Mookie Betts
3B: Max Muncy
LF: Teoscar Hernández
CF: Andy Pages
RF: Kyle Tucker
DH: Shohei Ohtani
Bench: Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim*
*If the Dodgers carry 14 position players
Dodgers pitching staff locks
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips
The Dodgers' starting rotation is set, assuming no further setbacks with Blake Snell's groin injury. The back end of the bullpen has come into focus, too, with Tanner Scott and/or Roki Sasaki the most logical candidates to serve as closer, and Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips separating themselves as the team's next most-trusted high-leverage relief options.
The only real question here is how the Dodgers will line up the rotation. Yamamoto-Skubal would make sense for Games 1 and 2 of a division series (keeping them both on-line for a potential Game 5). But could Tyler Glasnow's potential issues with traveling tempt the Dodgers to use him primarily at home, if they can? All factors to consider in the coming weeks.
Pitching staff questions
Roster bubble candidates: Brock Stewart, Edwin Díaz, Blake Treinen, Kris Bubic, Jack Dreyer, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, Eric Lauer
The first thing the Dodgers need to figure out here is health.
Edgardo Henriquez will almost certainly be on the playoff roster, and pitching in a high-leverage role, if he can make a full recovery from his recent back strain. Will Klein and Eric Lauer might also be available health-wise, though lack clear roles to step immediately back into.
Otherwise, the Dodgers will effectively have at least four open spots for six to seven other pitchers.
For added right-handed depth, they might be deciding between Brock Stewart (who has been a go-to weapon against right-handed hitters recently), Edwin Díaz (who is trying to salvage his dismal debut season, and did throw a pair of scoreless outings this weekend) and Blake Treinen (who has curiously pitched only five times in three weeks since being activated from the injured list, and not in the highest of leverage).
For another left-handed option, they could go with Kris Bubic (the trade deadline acquisition who has impressed with three scoreless appearances since returning from an injury) or Jack Dreyer (who was one of the Dodgers' best relievers from June to August, but has given up five runs in his last seven outings).
And for a multi-inning role, they will have Emmet Sheehan (who has looked like a different pitcher in three sterling starts since returning from a minor-league demotion) and Justin Wrobleski (the breakout All-Star who has finally shaken some of his home run problems since moving to the bullpen).
There are many permutations that the Dodgers could employ depending on opponent. They're still figuring out the exact hierarchy of all their bullpen arms, too.
But as long as their rotation is dominant, everything else should take care of itself.
Pitching staff projection
Rotation: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Bullpen: Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Kris Bubic, Edwin Díaz, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski

Why Dodgers have MLB's top-ranked playoff rotation even without Shohei Ohtani originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers got some tough news in early July when Shohei Ohtani was taken off the mound and forced into a DH-only role for a while.
With his attempt to return to the mound not going well, he's not expected to pitch again for the Dodgers this season. When he comes back off the IL, he'll slot into the DH role as usual. But the Dodgers' rotation is more than capable without him.
ESPN's Kiley McDaniel ranked the Dodgers' rotation as the best in baseball, even if Ohtani isn't there. The reason why is simple: Los Angeles is stacked with starting pitchers, both in terms of high-end options and depth pieces.
Why Dodgers' rotation is best in MLB for playoffs even without Shohei Ohtani
"Yep, the Dodgers are still tops in this category -- even with the currently injured Shohei Ohtani likely not pitching again this season -- and by a pretty good margin," McDaniel writes. "They could start four arms over a seven-game series that are all better than any one arm on five or six of the teams listed below."
Of all the postseason teams this year, the Dodgers' rotation has four starters who could be those teams' No. 1 starting pitchers.
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are the Dodgers' best starters, and they'd likely be the Game 1 and Game 2 starters if the Dodgers could choose who takes the mound.
After those two are Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell, two incredible starters who have a very high ceiling and would be the No. 1 starter for teams like the San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, and Chicago White Sox.
That four-man starting rotation is probably more than good enough to consider this Dodgers' rotation the best in baseball. But they also have some incredible depth options.
Justin Wrobleski is an incredible No. 5 starter. Kris Bubic and Emmett Sheehan probably won't start a playoff game for the Dodgers, but they would be capable No. 4 starting pitchers on most playoff teams.
For the Dodgers, those two are likely to be key bullpen arms. That's not to mention Roki Sasaki, who's going to return to the bullpen for the Dodgers in October as they look to win a third straight title.
The Dodgers have eight starting pitching options that could reasonably start a playoff game, and no one would bat an eye. It's an incredibly deep rotation, and that's without factoring in Ohtani. That's how good this rotation is. No other team can compare.

Will Roki Sasaki again be the Dodgers’ closer in the playoffs?
The Dodgers have created a pathway to make that possible, as manager Dave Roberts said that Sasaki will be moved into the bullpen when he is activated from the injured list this week.
Sasaki has pitched in 23 games this season, every one of them starts. A blister on his pitching hand has sidelined him since Aug. 27, but Roberts said he expected him to be activated during an upcoming three-game series against the Padres that starts on Tuesday.
The Dodgers had refrained from turning Sasaki into a reliever up to this point because of concerns over their starting rotation. Blake Snell departed from his most recent start after one inning because of a tight groin, but the two-time Cy Young Award winner has since not experienced any problems in that area.
The team believes it has four healthy starters in Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow. Emmet Sheehan figures to be the rotation’s new insurance policy, as Sheehan has allowed only one run in 17 innings pitched this month.
Roberts said he doesn’t plan to use Sasaki as a quasi-starter who pitches four or five innings following an opener.
Asked if Sasaki would be used in late-inning, high-leverage situations, Roberts replied, “I trust Roki in any situation. I would say probably start a clean inning, but, yeah.”
Could he close?
“It won’t be the ninth inning the first time,” Roberts said.
But Roberts acknowledged there was a chance Sasaki could end up in that role.
Sasaki became the Dodgers’ closer last year by default, as the team didn’t have any other options. He saved three games in the postseason.
His move to the bullpen last year came after he missed 4 ½ months because of shoulder problems. He agreed to try pitching in relief under the condition the Dodgers let him start again the next season.
Sasaki is 5-5 with a 4.70 earned-run average this year, but was 2-0 with a 3.05 ERA in the seven starts he made after the All-Star break.
The Dodgers started this season counting on $69-million free agent addition Edwin Diaz to be their closer, but the three-time All-Star has endured a nightmare of a season that has included two IL stints. In Diaz’s absence, Tanner Scott has served as the team’s primary ninth-inning option and has performed well. However, Scott has posted a 4.97 ERA over his last 14 games.

The Dodgers are taking advantage of the schedule in front of them, with 14 wins in 19 September games, including winning the last 10 in a row at home. This week that meant beating the Reds three times in four games in Cincinnati, then returning to Los Angeles to sweep the Giants.
They went with a two-way under the Cincinnati skyline, first clinching a postseason berth on Monday, tying the Atlanta Braves record with 14 straight postseasons, followed by winning their fifth straight National League West title and 13 out of 14 on Thursday.
Entering the final week of the season, the Dodgers can clinch a bye week with a magic number of three over the Braves.
Batter of the week
Kyle Tucker is starting to turn things around at the plate, and followed up an excellent series the previous weekend in Miami with nine hits in 20 at-bats, with three home runs and two doubles, with six walks and just one strikeout.
Honorable mention goes to Mookie Betts, who tied a Dodgers record with three doubles on Saturday, part of a stretch of three consecutive games with at least three hits. Will Smith found his power again with two home runs and a double, and Alex Freeland reached base eight times in 14 trips to the plate, including a home run and a double.
Pitcher of the week
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven scoreless innings with seven strikeouts to beat the Reds on Tuesday, his third straight seven-inning start in September. Yamamoto this season has allowed zero or one run in 14 of his 27 starts.
Honorable mention goes to Justin Wrobleski, who retired all nine batters he faced with three strikeouts while starting Thursday’s division clincher in Cincinnati, and to Landon Knack, who got the win in that game with four scoreless innings in relief. Also to Emmet Sheehan, who continued his strong six-week run with nine strikouts in 5 1/3 scoreless frames on Sunday.

Miscellany
Half a hundred: The Dodgers have won 10 games in a row at home, and Sunday’s win was their 50th win at Dodger Stadium this season. That’s six straight years with 50 wins at home, plus seven straight full seasons dating back to 2019. Since moving into Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers won 50 home games 12 times in 51 full seasons through 2014. But since 2015, they’ve won at least 50 games at home 10 times in 11 full seasons.
A crowded 10-K: Tyler Glasnow beat the Giants on Friday with a strong six innings, including 10 strikeouts. Glasnow is the eighth different Dodgers pitcher with a 10-strikeout game this season, the most in franchise history. No other MLB team this year has more than five such pitchers.
Parliamentary procedure: After making the All-Star team as a starter with the Kansas City Royals in 2025, left-hander Kris Bubic was on the 60-day injured list when the Dodgers acquired him just ahead of the August 3 trade deadline. Now he’s pitching in relief, angling for a spot on the postseason roster. With his appearance on Wednesday, Bubic became the 33rd different Dodgers pitcher used this season. So far, Bubic has four strikeouts in 2 2/3 innings in three appearances. “It’s just funk,” manager Dave Roberts said Sunday of Bubic. “It’s nothing overpowering, but there’s just funky swings, soft contact. I see him as a neutral pitcher, gets left and right out. I like those converted starters, because he knows how to navigate lineups.”
A quirk: The division clincher Thursday in Cincinnati was an 8-2 win, then came four home runs in the eighth inning Friday on the 20th anniversary of the 4+1 Game for another 8-2 triumph. That was the first time in Dodgers history they’ve won consecutive games by an 8-2 score.
Transactions
Monday: The fresh arm express was busy this week, beginning with Emmet Sheehan getting optioned the day after pitching six scoreless innings, in favor of Paul Gervase.
Monday: One day after a rare bad outing, Edgardo Henriquez was placed on the injured list with low back discomfort, ending his regular season and putting his playoff availability in question. Bobby Miller returned from Triple-A.
Wednesday: Trade deadline acquisition Kris Bubic was activated off the 60-day IL to make his Dodgers debut in relief, the team’s 33rd pitcher of the season. Gervase was optioned and Ryan Ward was designated for assignment.
Thursday: Miller was sent back to Oklahoma City, and Landon Knack was called up to pitch four scoreless innings in relief in the division clincher in Cincinnati.
Sunday: Sheehan got the call back up to the Dodgers, with Tarik Skubal placed on the bereavement list. Kyle Hurt was also called up, with Seth Halvorsen optioned.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers considering Emmet Sheehan for playoff role after gem in win over Giants
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez

item.content:encoded:
Emmet Sheehan’s next start will be in the minor leagues.
The right-hander might be out of sight, but that doesn’t mean he will be out of mind.
His scheduled start Saturday for triple-A Oklahoma City in a Pacific Coast League playoff game is part of a design to prepare him to pitch for the Dodgers in October.
Sheehan has pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
His quote-unquote demotion came after he pitched 5 ⅓ scoreless innings in the Los Angeles Dodgers’ sweep-sealing 3–1 victory over the San Francisco Giants Sunday.
The game was the third Sheehan pitched this month for the Dodgers. His numbers in those three games: 17 innings pitched, one run allowed, 24 strikeouts, three walks.
“I’ve loved the version we’ve seen of Emmet the last three outings,” manager Dave Roberts said. “He’s been fantastic.”
Sent down to Oklahoma City in early August, Sheehan returned to the major leagues earlier this month with a slightly modified arsenal that has significantly improved his results. He’s thrown his curveball more, and his increased inability to change speeds has made his fastball play up even when he’s not touching 97 mph with it.
“I think that obviously there’s a 97 that plays better, but 94–95 commanded still misses bats,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s something that, that’s one part of it. The other part of it is holding the velocity. And so, for me, the last three or four since he’s been back here, he’s held those 94s and 95s for the, call it, 85 pitches.”
With the Dodgers expecting to start Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow in the postseason, the team has started the process of moving Sheehan into a relief role by having Jack Dreyer pitch an inning as opener Sunday. Sheehan was down in triple-A over the last week but a roster spot for him was opened up because Skubal went on the bereavement list.
Sheehan entered the game in the second inning and pitched into the seventh. He gave up only one hit and one walk; he struck out nine.
He said he has made it a point to feel “free and easy” with his delivery.
“Instead of saying, ‘I need 97 [mph] here,’ it’s more like, ‘If I hit my spot, he’s not going to hit it,’” Sheehan said.
What it means
The teams with the two-best records in each league will earn a first-round bye and the Dodgers are close to wrapping up one of those spots. With their win over the Giants, the Dodgers maintained a four-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the National League’s No. 2 seed. Both teams have only six games remaining in the regular season.
Who’s hot
Left-hander Kris Bubic, who was acquired from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline, replaced Sheehan in the seventh inning and registered the final two outs of the inning. Bubic struck out Scott Bandura, only for Shay Whitcomb to reach base on a throwing error by Max Muncy.
No problem: Bubic forced Grant McCray to fly out to left field.
Bubic has pitched 2 ⅔ innings in three appearances for the Dodgers over the last week, and he still hasn’t allowed a run. He has struck out four.
Roberts said he’s also pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
“It’s nothing overpowering, but there’s just funky swings, soft contact,” Roberts said. “I see him as a neutral pitcher, gets left and right out, and I like those converted starters because he knows how to navigate lineups.”
Who’s Not
For today, this section should be renamed “Who Wasn’t Hot.”
The label certainly applied to Tommy Edman, who was two for his last 42 before his sixth-inning at-bat: That’s when Edman jumped on an inside cutter from Carson Seymour and launched it into the visiting bullpen behind the right-field wall.
Edman’s home run tied the game at 1–1.
Up next
The Dodgers have a day off Monday. They will resume play Tuesday when they host the San Diego Padres, who will send No. 1 starter Michael King (12-9, 3.03 ERA) to the mound. The Dodgers won’t have a traditional starter, as Roberts said the team is planning for a bullpen game.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will move right-hander Roki Sasaki to the bullpen when he returns from the injured list in their next series against the San Diego Padres.
Sasaki, 24, landed on the injured list at the end of August, putting an end to a dominant run which came after the All-Star break. He allowed two runs or fewer in each of his appearances leading into an Aug. 26 start against the Atlanta Braves, during which he allowed four earned runs.
Why Would the Dodgers Move Roki Sasaki to a Relief Role?
The Dodgers have to trim their rotation to four players when the postseason comes, so putting Sasaki back into the bullpen is only natural given the other players they have on their roster.
Tyler Glasnow, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are all likely to remain starters, so Sasaki’s relief role isn’t especially surprising. Roberts revealed Sasaki could operate in slightly different situations upon his return, potentially handling several innings in relief.
“I could see multiple innings but it’s not gonna be bulk like 4 or 5 innings,” Roberts said, per Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez.
“…I trust Roki in any situation. [His first appearance] won’t be in the ninth the first time. It could potentially fall out, but it won’t be that way.”
Sasaki has the stuff to be a high-leverage reliever and showed he was more than capable last season. His fastball ranks among the fastest in MLB, topping out above 100 mph, and his limited arsenal suggests he’ll see even more success as a reliever.
How Did Roki Sasaki Perform Out of the Bullpen Last Season?
Sasaki returned from a long-term stint on the injured list towards the latter end of last season. He made two appearances before the end of the year as a reliever, holding opponents scoreless in both before entering the postseason in the same role.
The right-hander looked like a brand new pitcher in the postseason, making nine appearances and only allowing one earned run through 10.2 innings pitched.
He took over as the team’s closer during their postseason run, and went 3-for-3 in save opportunities throughout October.
The Dodgers will hope he can find that same form in the bullpen this year as they chase a historic three-peat.

Is it still a rivalry? Dodgers complete sweep of woeful Giants
- Click here to listen to this article
-
Only the Pirates and Cubs have met more often than the Dodgers and Giants, who faced off for the first time in 1889. And over all that time, the Dodgers are just two games better, with 1,294 wins to the Giants’ 1,292.
The Dodgers and Giants have also won more pennants, made more World Series appearances and have more players wearing their caps in the Hall of Fame than any other National League teams, all of which fueled a rivalry that was once among the most visceral and passionate in American sports.
But that was then and this is now.
After Sunday’s 3-1 victory over the Giants, the Dodgers’ 14th win in their last 17 games, the team could finish a season with 100 wins for the fourth time in six years. The Giants have had just one winning record in that time.
The Dodgers (96-60), who have won five straight division titles, are headed to the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year. The Giants will miss the playoffs for a fifth straight season.
So is the rivalry dead? That depends on who you ask.
“It’s always a rivalry,” Giants pitcher Logan Webb. “We’d like to make it a little closer when it comes to the standings. But I definitely feel it when I throw against them.”
But then Webb, who is from Northern California, grew up with the rivalry and, as the longest-tenured Giant, pitched against the Dodgers in games that mattered. Giants coach Ron Washington, who made his major league debut with the Dodgers when the rivalry was still a thing, said many players on San Francisco’s roster don’t know that background.
Mookie Betts hits three doubles and the Dodgers piled up 15 hits in a 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants with Shohei Ohtani’s return on the horizon.
“It should be a rivalry. But I don’t think the young kids we got know anything about a rivalry. They’re not history buffs.”
Webb said it’s the responsibility of the veterans on both sides to keep that history alive by explaining the enmity to the young players.
“I think there are still guys that came up in the system that know what it’s like,” he said. “It’s my job to kind of hype these guys up to play a game like this.”
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who played for the Dodgers and Giants during his 10-year career, agrees the rivalry now exists more in the history books than the current standings, where the Giants have been overtaken by the San Diego Padres, who will finish second to the Dodgers in the N.L. West for the fourth time in five seasons.
“It’s certainly a rivalry in the sense of the history, the fan bases,” Roberts said. “But obviously it’s about relevancy. The Padres have been successful the last handful of years, and so it’s certainly built some momentum. The geography lends itself to that too.
“But Dodgers Giants is always fun.”
It hasn’t been so much fun for the Giants lately. San Francisco hasn’t won the season series with the Dodgers since 2021 and has lost more than 90 games this year for the first time in nine seasons.
On Sunday they went in front three batters into the game with Johan Cox working Dodger opener Jack Dreyer for a leadoff walk, then making his way around the bases on Dreyer’s throwing error, a stolen base and a one-one single by Victor Bericoto.
But San Francisco didn’t get another hit until Jung Hoo Lee singled with one out in the sixth.
That allowed the Dodgers to tie the score in the sixth on Tommy Edman’s seventh home run of the season just inside the right-field foul pole. An inning later they went ahead to stay when Max Muncy singled under a sliding Cox at second, moved to third on a single by rookie Josue De Paula and scored on Kiké Hernández’s double to center.
A two-out single by Muncy, his second of the game, scored Teoscar Hernández, who also had two hits, in the eighth inning with the final run.
Even the slumping Freddie Freeman contributed to the Dodgers’ 11-hit attack, ending an 0-for-11 slide with a broken-bat single in the fourth then singling again in the eighth.
Sunday’s result helped clarify the Dodgers’ once-muddy playoff picture. With six games left in the regular season, the Dodgers lead Atlanta by four games in the race for the second seed in the National League playoffs, which would give them a first-round bye and the homefield advantage in the division series.
The team’s postseason roster may be getting clearer as well. Right-hander Emmet Sheehan, who made 22 starts this season, came out of the bullpen for the first time Sunday and was brilliant in his audition for the playoffs.
“If there is a role in the postseason, it will be out of the [bull]pen,” Roberts said of Sheehan, who gave up just a hit and walk, striking out nine — one off his season high — in 5 1/3 innings.
Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title.
De Paula, meanwhile, who also doubled in running his modest hitting streak to four games, appears to have secured a job as the team’s left-handed bat off the bench while utility player Hyeseong Kim, who has spent the last four months in the minors, will rejoin the Dodgers after the triple-A playoffs and be considered for a roster spot as a pinch-runner and late-inning defensive replacement.
“My expectation is that Hyeseong will be here during the off week and potentially be a conversation for the postseason because he has the ability to run, play defense, and steal a base,” Roberts said.
After Monday’s off day, the final break of the regular season for the Dodgers, the team is expected to activate Andy Pages, Roki Sasaki and Shohei Ohtani from the injured list during its three-game series with the Padres.

LOS ANGELES -- The saying goes that pitching wins championships, and that was true in different ways when the Dodgers won back-to-back World Series in 2024 and '25.
The 2024 Dodgers had to lean heavily on their bullpen out of necessity, while the '25 team rode its rotation to a successful title defense -- so much so that all four starting pitchers took the ball in the winner-take-all Game 7.
As the Dodgers go for a three-peat this year, they'll once again look for their starting four of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow to set the tone. But their bullpen feels less volatile than it was last year, and it could be one of the most fluid position groups as L.A. considers how to piece together its postseason rosters.
One way or another, the Dodgers will carry their best 13 pitchers in the postseason, because as manager Dave Roberts has said repeatedly, like a mantra: "Every inning in the postseason is leverage."
The Dodgers got a look at several postseason 'pen candidates when they ran a bullpen game to success on Sunday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, capping a three-game sweep of the Giants with a 3-1 victory. Right-hander Emmet Sheehan struck out nine in 5 1/3 scoreless innings of bulk relief, giving L.A. an intriguing option to add to the mix.
The Dodgers' fourth straight victory maintained their four-game lead over the Braves for the second-best record in the National League -- and a first-round postseason bye -- with six games left to play.
The greatest need in the bullpen is right-handed leverage arms. Edwin Díaz, who signed a three-year, $69 million deal to be their closer, has been relegated to lower leverage for the time being amid his poor performance in an injury-ravaged season. Edgardo Henriquez, who stepped up to become L.A.'s most reliable righty in leverage, is out for the rest of the regular season due to a lower back strain. He could return during the postseason, but the uncertainty still creates a need.
Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart have been solid options, but they have been more valuable as part of the bridge to the ninth inning, rather than to close out games. In order to find such options from the right-hand side, the Dodgers can turn to the strength of their staff: the rotation.
Sheehan is one candidate, although he'll remain stretched out through the end of the regular season as rotation depth. Another is Roki Sasaki, who was also originally going to remain built up as a starter upon his return from the 15-day IL. Instead, Roberts said, Sasaki will likely be activated Tuesday and be available out of the bullpen, beginning his transition to relief in the final days of the regular season.
"He's done it. He's really good. He's a neutral pitcher, high-octane stuff," Roberts said. "You really just need four starters, you know. So we're in a good spot there for now."
Sheehan and Sasaki both got a crash course in short-burst relief last fall. While Sasaki thrived as the Dodgers' postseason closer, Sheehan was scored on in his first four appearances before rebounding for scoreless outings in Games 3 and 7 of the World Series.
For Sheehan, adapting his typical routine to relief was difficult, but he believes that he can build on last year if he gets the call to the 'pen again.
"Having that experience helps a lot," Sheehan said. "Just getting back into that, I know what I need to do to get ready to go into the game."
And don't count out Díaz. His pitch to earn a spot in the postseason 'pen began with two scoreless innings against the Giants this weekend.
When the postseason comes, the Dodgers may not be able to avoid using Díaz in leverage, even if they don't throw him into a comparable situation in the final days of the regular season. But if he shows enough this week, then L.A. will bet on his track record.
"I gotta show them I’m part of that bullpen," Díaz said. "I haven’t pitched [much] this year, and when I’ve been on the mound I’ve been struggling. So right now, I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot."

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal is going on the bereavement list, manager Dave Roberts announced on Sunday.
The move came a day after Skubal suffered his worst start with the Dodgers, giving up four runs in five innings in Saturday’s 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants.
In his absence, Emmet Sheehan was called up from triple-A, returning in hopes of building off back-to-back strong starts earlier this month. He will follow opener Jack Dreyer on Sunday as the bulk pitcher for the Dodgers’ series finale with the Giants.
Roberts said Skubal would be away from the Dodgers for “a couple days.” No further information on his situation was available.
Skubal is a contender to be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter in the playoffs, after being acquired in a blockbuster deal at the trade deadline in August. Even after Saturday’s setback, in which he allowed eight hits and bemoaned his lack of fastball command, the left-hander is 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA in nine starts with the Dodgers this season.
The two-time Cy Young Award winner will anchor a postseason rotation also expected to include Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell (assuming he continues to recover from his recent groin injury).
The Dodgers also freshened up their bullpen on Sunday, swapping out right-handers was calling up Kyle Hurt and optioning Seth Halvorsen.
The team enters Sunday with the chance to not only sweep the Giants, but further lower their current magic number of four to secure a first-round bye in the playoffs.
They enter play on Sunday four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League.

The Los Angeles Dodgers starting rotation is so good collectively when they are healthy that it's sometimes difficult to focus on the individuals' accomplishments.
As a fan, it's easy to just look at the starting unit of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Shohei Ohtani as one. But Yamamoto's latest feat stands out even relative to this dominant group of pitchers.
Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been dominant this season
Yamamoto's most recent start came on September 15 against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. It was yet another ho-hum performance by the Dodgers ace. He picked up the win going seven scoreless innings, while allowing just one hit. He only walked two batters while striking out seven. Yamamoto lowered his career WHIP to 0.96, which is officially the best WHIP ever by a pitcher their first 75 career starts.
Yamamoto outpaced 2025 National League Cy Young Award-winner — and perhaps future Dodgers pitcher in Paul Skenes — as well as former member of LA's pitching staff, Walker Buehler. Behind Yamamoto, Skenes, and Buehler are Seattle Mariners All-Star starter Bryan Woo and Tampa Bay Rays right-hander Drew Rasmussen.
Not only does Yamamoto have the best WHIP ever through his first 75 games, but he's allowed the third-fewest runs in MLB history by a pitcher through that same span (trailing only Rasmussen and Skenes).
Opposing hitters are hitting .192/.252/.310 against Yamamoto through those 75 starts -- that is the lowest batting average against of any pitcher since 1974 (when that data became available). It's also the lowest on-base percentage, the fifth-lowest slugging percentage, and the second-lowest OPS.
Below is a list of fewest hits allowed in MLB history by a pitcher in their first 75 starts. There's a lot of familiar names on that list.
| Pitcher | Hits Allowed |
|---|---|
| 1. Tony Gonsolin (LAD) | 264 |
| 2. Freddy Peralta (MIL) | 270 |
| 3. Drew Rasmussen (TB) | 284 |
| T-4. Cristian Javier (HOU) | 287 |
| T-4. Edward Cabrera (MIA) | 287 |
| 6. Triston McKenzie (CLE) | 295 |
| 7. Jack Flaherty (STL) | 299 |
| T-8. Yoshinobu Yamamoto (LAD) | 305 |
| T-8. Shohei Ohtani (LAA) | 305 |
| 10. Tyler Glasnow (LAD) | 313 |
Yamamoto has clearly been worth every penny since he signed that mega-deal with the Dodgers. It's nice to be able to point to his historic regular season success as well as his historic postseason success. Yamamoto is slowly building up a Hall of Fame résumé through his first three Major League seasons.

item.content:encoded:
2026 looked to be a lost season for Mookie Betts, as an oblique injury cost him a month’s worth of time. At the All-Star break, the Dodgers shortstop was limping to the tune of a .235/.293/.416 slashline with 11 home runs and 31 RBI over 60 games.
Since the second half of the regular season began, Betts has turned into his 2023 MVP-runner-up self, as he’s slashing .290/.364/.452 with 11 home runs and 36 RBI over his last 56 games. Betts has been on a tear his last three games, as he’s hitting .833 with five extra-base hits and five RBI, highlighted by a four-hit, three-double game on Saturday in the Dodgers’ 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants.
Betts has hit all around the lineup, going from as high as leadoff to as low as the six hole, but Betts has been certifying himself as a force at the top of the lineup during this final homestand. Betts spoke with David Vassegh of SportsNet LA about his torrid stretch at the plate hitting at the top spot following Saturday’s win, noting that the return of Shohei Ohtani will directly impact where he hits everyday.
“It’s fun. Like you said, I’ve done it for so long, but that man Shohei— he deserves what he gets. We all know where he needs to hit in the lineup.”
Saturday was a rough outing for left-hander Tarik Skubal as he allowed four earned runs while striking out a season-low three hitters over five innings.
Despite the atypical night for Skubal, his offense was able to generate six runs after his final pitch, giving him his fourth win as a Dodger. When speaking with Vassegh following the game, Skubal gave all the credit to the offense and bullpen for carrying the team the rest of the way.
“Obviously, I wasn’t very good today. The offense, defense and bullpen picked me up big time, and that’s what good teams do— they pick each other up, and win series and win baseball games. Hats off to them.”
Mirjam Swanson at the Los Angeles Times writes about Tyler Glasnow and the ability to trust himself as the playoffs loom near. Glasnow was solid on Friday against San Francisco, allowing just two runs while striking out 10 hitters.
“Today was a step in the right direction,” said Glasnow, the formerHart High star, before leaving the clubhouse in flip-flops. “I’d rather kind of feel it, work through some stuff, and have a good one right before playoffs.
“I think I’m in a good spot right now.”
Jack Harris of the California Post has a positive update regarding Shohei Ohtani, as the two-way superstar did base running drills and used the Trajekt Ark pitching machine in the cage. Hitting coach Aaron Bates notes that Ohtani has been really good with the machine, and the next test will be how he performs in live batting practice.
“In the cage, in a controlled setting, he’s been really good. It’s 100% intensity,” Bates said. “Once he gets out to the field, if he does a live BP or something like that, and the intensity ramps up, it’ll be a good test to see what happens. But in the cage, in the controlled setting, he’s been really good.”

- Mookie Betts hits three doubles and the Dodgers surge for 15 hits to overcome a shaky start by Tarik Skubal in a 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants.
When Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said earlier this week that the best was yet to come, his expectations were centered on the offense.
In the Dodgers’ 10-4 rout of the San Francisco Giants on Saturday, that better version of the offense was on display, putting together a pair of three-run rallies in back-to-back innings to take pressure off the pitching staff.
Before that breakout started in the fifth inning, it was a back-and-forth game.
Dodgers left-handed starting pitcher Tarik Skubal pitched only five innings, tied for his shortest start with the Dodgers. And he surrendered four runs, the worst mark of his Dodgers tenure.
Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title.
Entering the game, Skubal appeared to be peaking. His last two starts, both against the Reds, were some of his most efficient.
That efficiency, however, regressed against the Giants (64-91).
Though he got through the first two innings without giving up a run — thanks in part to a diving catch by right fielder Kyle Tucker made in the gap to end the first — he issued two-out walks in each.
The Dodgers’ offense used that time to mount a lead. Leadoff hitter Mookie Betts, who finished the day with three doubles and a single, hit the first of those doubles in his first at-bat, and Max Muncy authored his own to drive in the first run.
The next inning, rookie Josue De Paula’s walk, and singles from Alex Freeland and Betts combined to push in another run.
Then Skubal began to struggle. With a runner on second and one out, he pitched to a full count against designated hitter Victor Bericoto. Skubal missed down the middle with a fastball, and Bericoto sent it 425 feet to center field. It landed on the netting on the other side of the wall to tie the score.
The Dodgers’ offense, coming alive in September, struck back in the third. Catcher Will Smith hit his second home run in as many nights, launching the second pitch of the frame into left-field stands.
The Giants took a different approach to tie the score for a second time. After back-to-back singles, they used back-to-back sacrifice bunts to advance the runners and score another run.
Then the two teams traded runs again. Betts put the Dodgers (95-60) up with an RBI double in the fourth. Skubal gave up back-to-back doubles in the fifth.
That marked both the end of Skubal’s start and the beginning of the Dodgers’ offensive onslaught.
If the man trying to revive the Montreal Expos as an expansion team succeeds, Dan Evans is his choice for president of baseball operations.
The Dodgers brought seven batters to the plate in the fifth, and all but one reached base. Tommy Edman hit a two-run single. And pinch-hitting Miguel Rojas almost matched him, but Giants left fielder Turner Hill made a perfect throw to nab Edman in a close play at home to end the inning.
Betts’ and Smith’s bats stayed hot to open the sixth with a leadoff double and one-out RBI single, respectively. The Dodgers took advantage of the Giants’ sloppy infield play to load the bases for De Paula, who lined a two-run single into shallow center field.
Those were the kinds of stifling rallies that had defined the Dodgers offense earlier in the season, when they were scoring regularly in double digits.
The Dodgers’ 15 hits Saturday were their most in a game since July 2 against the San Diego Padres, and just two shy of their season high.

item.content:encoded:
- Los Angeles Dodgers. Dodgers facing nightmare playoff decision over Edwin Díaz as October looms
- Los Angeles Dodgers. “They basically lie”: Shohei Ohtani accused of hiding multiple injuries to avoid being placed on Dodgers' injured list
Shohei Ohtani’s path back to the Los Angeles Dodgers lineup is becoming clearer, and manager Dave Roberts has provided another encouraging sign as the club prepares for October.
Ohtani took coach-pitch batting practice Friday after beginning his hitting progression with tee work earlier in the week. The Dodgers’ four-time MVP remains on the 15-day injured list with left-knee and right-biceps issues, but his recent activity has given the club reason for optimism.
Roberts said Ohtani came through the latest workout well and described the past several days as productive. However, the manager stressed that the slugger hasn’t yet advanced to live batting practice or work with the Trajekt pitching simulator.
“He came out of it well,” Roberts said. “I think for me, I'm just really waiting to hear when he's going to get on the field, let alone take live BP or Trajekt.
“And he's not there yet. But everything I've heard, it's been a really productive last three to four to five days. He's in a good spot.”
Before Ohtani returns to game action, Roberts wants him to face roughly 10 to 12 at-bats against pitching.
That timetable matters. Ohtani’s IL stint was backdated to Sept. 8, making Sept. 23 the earliest activation date. If he’s ready by then, he’ll have only five regular-season games to regain his timing before the postseason begins.
Dodgers’ offense keeps rolling without Ohtani
The Dodgers have managed his absence effectively, winning six of nine games and averaging 5.3 runs per contest during that stretch. Their latest victory showed just how much offensive depth remains available while Ohtani recovers.
Los Angeles defeated the San Francisco Giants 8-2 on Friday, with Mookie Betts homering twice and the Dodgers launching four home runs in the eighth inning.
Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker went back-to-back before Betts and Will Smith followed with consecutive blasts. Tyler Glasnow also delivered six innings with 10 strikeouts.
The performance underscored why the Dodgers can afford to be patient with Ohtani rather than rushing his return. Still, his presence would add another major dimension to a lineup already producing at a high level.
Before landing on the injured list, Ohtani hit .296 with 26 home runs and a .952 OPS across 110 games. He struggled over his final 24 games, batting .198 with a .690 OPS and 34 strikeouts, making the decision to pause his workload especially significant.
Ohtani’s return date remains unconfirmed, but the progression from tee work to coach-pitch batting practice represents another step forward.
With Los Angeles already having secured the NL West, the priority is getting its superstar healthy and ready to contribute when the games carry their greatest postseason significance.

item.content:encoded:
Tyler Glasnow on Friday night struck out 10 Giants in his six innings, his most in a start this season. Aside from securing Los Angeles-area folks a free Jumbo Jack with a purchase of a large drink for the 130th time this season and the 27th time in the last 28 days, Friday affirmed the Dodgers’ unique spot in double-digit strikeout games this season.
The Dodgers now have a dozen individual 10-strikeout games this season. That’s not the most, it’s tied for fourth-most with the Toronto Blue Jays, behind the Milwaukee Brewers (16), Cleveland Guardians (15), and Philadelphia Phillies (14).
But what makes the Dodgers unique this season is that eight different pitchers have achieved double-digit strikeouts in a game:
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto (May 31, July 4, September 9)
- Emmet Sheehan (April 24, September 7)
- Blake Snell (August 11, August 29)
- Shohei Ohtani (April 15)
- Roki Sasaki (June 5)
- Justin Wrobleski (June 30)
- Tarik Skubal (August 22)
- Tyler Glasnow (September 18)
The next-closest team is the Minnesota Twins, with five different pitchers striking out at least 10 in a game this season. The Houston Astros, Brewers, New York Yankees, Pittsburgh Pirates, Texas Rangers, and Seattle Mariners have four pitchers each.
The Dodgers have eight different pitchers, which is at least one measure of their depth.
Eight pitchers with 10 strikeouts is the most the Dodgers have ever had in a season, two more than in 2022.

Los Ángeles - Mookie Betts conectó dos jonrones y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles pegaron cuatro cuadrangulares en la octava entrada para imponerse 8-2 a los Giants de San Francisco la noche del viernes, en un partido que marcó el regreso desde la lista de lesionados del relevista puertorriqueño Edwin “Sugar” Díaz.
Max Muncy y Kyle Tucker conectaron jonrones consecutivos en la octava. Betts y Max Muncy añadieron vuelacercas solitarios con dos outs en una entrada de cinco carreras, mientras los campeones del Oeste de la Liga Nacional se impusieron en el primer juego de una serie entre viejos rivales.
Tyler Glasnow (5-1) permitió dos carreras y tres imparables en seis entradas, con un máximo de temporada de 10 ponches.
La lluvia de jonrones ocurrió en el vigésimo aniversario del juego de cuatro-más-uno de los Dodgers. Jeff Kent, J.D. Drew, Russell Martin y Marlon Anderson conectaron cuatro jonrones consecutivos en la parte baja de la novena entrada, la cuarta vez en la historia de las Grandes Ligas que se lograba esa hazaña.
El relevista de los Giants Philip Abner permitió las cinco carreras en la octava, que comenzó con los Dodgers arriba 3-2. Se convirtió en el segundo relevista en la historia de San Francisco en permitir cuatro jonrones en una misma entrada.
Los Giants (64-90) perdieron su juego número 90, su mayor cantidad desde 2017, cuando cayeron 98 veces.
El boricua Edwin Díaz ponchó a dos en una novena entrada sin carreras en su regreso desde la lista de lesionados.
Los Dodgers lo activaron desde la lista de lesionados de 15 días, donde había ingresado el 18 de agosto por una inflamación en el cuello. Fue su segunda vez en el año en la lista de lesionados, luego de una primera por problemas en el codo derecho.
El equipo no espera usar al relevista en situaciones de aprietos, pero con ventaja de seis carreras fue traído en la novena. De no haber sido por esa ventaja, admitió el dirigente Dave Roberts, no lo hubieran utilizado en la novena.
Provocó un elevado y ponchó a un bateador con un foul tip antes de permitir un sencillo con dos outs. Pero evitó cualquier daño, terminando el juego al hacer que Brett Harris hiciera swing a un slider difícil de batear. La recta de cuatro costuras de Díaz promedió 97.6 millas por hora (1.3 mph más que su promedio de la temporada), alcanzando un máximo de 98.7 millas.
“La recta tenía mucha vida”, dijo Roberts según publicó MLB.com. “Noventa y seis millas por hora es muy diferente a 99. Y parecía que su lanzamiento pasaba por el receptor, y la recta tenía esa potencia. Y luego el slider... una vez que tienes esa recta, el slider es bastante letal”.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers esperan que Snell (ingle) haga una apertura más antes de la postemporada
This browser does not support the video element.
LOS ÁNGELES -- Dos días después de salir de su apertura tras apenas una entrada debido a rigidez en la ingle izquierda, Blake Snell lanzó desde 90 pies de distancia en el terreno del Dodger Stadium antes del primer juego de la serie del viernes contra los Gigantes. Salió sintiéndose bien, y los Dodgers creen que evitaron lo peor con una lesión que ha sido un problema recurrente a lo largo de la carrera del zurdo.
"Feliz de que lo detectamos a tiempo", indicó el manager Dave Roberts, quien señaló que Snell no fue enviado a hacerse ninguna prueba de imagen.
Los Dodgers se mantienen optimistas de que el dos veces ganador del Premio Cy Young hará otra apertura en la temporada regular en algún momento durante sus nueve juegos restantes. El día específico está por verse -- su turno regular en la rotación caería durante la serie de tres choques de Los Ángeles ante San Diego que comienza el martes -- pero no se espera que lance con ninguna limitación.
"Creo que sería más una apertura normal", aseguró Roberts. "Tal vez no lo exijamos muchísimo, dado que no sabemos cómo se desarrollará la temporada. Pero esta será su última salida de la temporada regular, así que creo que sería más una apertura regular".
This browser does not support the video element.
Snell inició la campaña en la lista de lesionados de 15 días con fatiga en el hombro izquierdo, haciendo su debut de temporada apenas el 9 de mayo. Casi de inmediato volvió a la lista de lesionados debido a cuerpos libres en su codo izquierdo, los cuales fueron removidos mediante el procedimiento NanoNeedle Scope. Desde que regresó el 11 de agosto, Snell ha lucido como si no hubiera perdido el ritmo, registrando efectividad de 1.01 en siete aperturas, con 47 ponches y 14 bases por bolas en 35.2 entradas.
Para un lanzador que comparte la rotación con Yoshinobu Yamamoto y Tarik Skubal, Snell es una pieza absolutamente vital en los planes de los Dodgers para los playoffs. Si su condición empeora, la profundidad del pitcheo abridor de Los Ángeles de repente luce bastante mermada. Está Tyler Glasnow, quien abrió el viernes contra San Francisco pero que ha lidiado con sus propios problemas de lesiones este año. También se espera que Roki Sasaki (fuera desde el 27 de agosto por una ampolla en el dedo medio derecho) regrese pronto para una última apertura en la temporada regular.
Dada la historia de Snell de lanzar bien luego de largas ausencias de acción en Grandes Ligas, ¿han considerado los Dodgers permitirle saltarse su próxima apertura, que siga descansando y esperar a que vuelva a la loma una vez que comiencen los juegos de postemporada?
"Se ha pensado en eso", reveló Roberts. "Pero todavía estás hablando de unos posibles 17 días, algo así... es mucho tiempo para no estar en competencia. Donde normalmente, con su historial, todavía tienes rehabilitaciones y cosas por el estilo. Así que no es sólo cuestión de conectarlo y ya, que descanse dos semanas y lance en un juego de playoffs".

Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 8-2 a los Giants de San Francisco, impulsados por cinco jonrones y una gran actuación de Mookie Betts.
Los Dodgers comenzaron el encuentro con ventaja gracias a un jonrón solitario de Mookie Betts en la primera entrada.
San Francisco respondió en los siguientes episodios. Jung Hoo Lee conectó cuadrangular en la segunda entrada y posteriormente Jonah Cox produjo otra carrera con un sencillo, colocando a los Giants arriba 2-1.
Los locales lograron empatar en la quinta entrada mediante un sencillo productor de Teoscar Hernández. En el sexto episodio, un doblete de Josué De Paula permitió que Kyle Tucker anotara la carrera que puso nuevamente a Los Ángeles al frente.
El abridor de los Dodgers, Tyler Glasnow, tuvo una actuación destacada al lanzar seis entradas, permitir tres imparables y dos carreras, además de registrar 10 ponches.
Dodgers explotan con cinco carreras en la octava entrada
El partido se definió en la octava entrada, cuando Los Ángeles fabricó un rally de cinco carreras.
Max Muncy abrió la ofensiva con un cuadrangular solitario y Kyle Tucker siguió con otro jonrón para ampliar la ventaja.
Posteriormente, Mookie Betts conectó su segundo cuadrangular de la noche, esta vez con un corredor en circulación, para colocar el marcador 7-2.
La fiesta ofensiva terminó con un jonrón solitario de Will Smith, que puso el 8-2 definitivo. Los Dodgers conectaron cuatro cuadrangulares en esa entrada.
Betts terminó como una de las figuras del encuentro al conectar dos jonrones y producir tres carreras. Por su parte, Glasnow consiguió la victoria y elevó su registro de la temporada a 5-1.
Con el triunfo, los Dodgers mejoraron su marca a 94-60 y se mantienen en el primer lugar del Oeste de la Liga Nacional, mientras que San Francisco quedó con registro de 64-90.

Mookie Betts estuvo intratable con el madero para liderar la exhibición de poder de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, quienes se impusieron con un contundente 8-2 sobre los Gigantes de San Francisco. La ofensiva californiana se descargó con un total de cinco cuadrangulares en una velada especial para la franquicia.
El estelar bateador abrió la cuenta desde el primer episodio al conectar su bambinazo número 21 del año por el callejón del jardín izquierdo-central. Más adelante, en el octavo tramo, volvió a conectar un batazo de cuatro esquinas con un corredor a bordo para registrar su cuadrangular 22 de la temporada y redondear una noche importante a la ofensiva.
El despliegue de fuerza sirvió como conmemoración de los 20 años del emblemático juego del “4+1”, una de las remontadas más recordadas en la historia de la organización. Los bateadores de los Dodgers emularon aquel hecho desatando un vendaval de batazos para asegurar la victoria.

En lo individual, Betts terminó la jornada de 4-3 con dos cuadrangulares, tres carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas recibida, méritos suficientes para ser nombrado el Jugador del Partido. Desde la lomita, Tyler Glasnow se adjudicó el triunfo tras una buena labor, mientras que la derrota recayó en Jason Foley.
Con esta victoria de local, los Dodgers alcanzaron las 94 victorias en la campaña para mantenerse firmes en la cima de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional, poniéndose a tono cara a los playoffs.

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The oft-injured Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title.
- Glasnow fought through early struggles to throw six innings and strike out 10 in an 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants, but can he replicate that in the playoffs?
- The veteran right-hander played a key role in the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series, and the team will need him to do the same this October.
The Dodgers are all in, going for a three-peat.
And they might not have an extra ace up their sleeve anymore, but when the postseason begins, they’ll still hope to play their quad of aces — four of a kind that will beat almost every other hand.
But do the Dodgers have four aces? Or three? Or just a pair, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal?
Could the left groin tightness that chased Blake Snell from his last start after an inning linger into the postseason? Snell isn’t the sturdiest of starters, having missed most of the season because of shoulder fatigue and loose bodies in his left elbow. But the Dodgers suggest he’s going to be OK; Snell is slated for one last regular-season start.
And what about Tyler Glasnow?
Tyler Glasnow gives up just three hits and strikes out 10, and Mookie Betts hits two home runs in the Dodgers’ 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants.
Can the Dodgers trust the 6-foot-8 right-hander who missed three months because of back spasms?
Should they put their belief in the 11th-year pitcher who likely would be the odd man out in the postseason if Shohei Ohtani still were available to deal on the mound?
They’re going to have to trust Glasnow. And he’s going to have to trust himself.
“He’s a guy that you can’t put too much thought into him, or it starts getting in his own head,” said catcher Dalton Rushing, who is injured but enjoyed watching Glasnow find his footing in Friday’s 8-2 victory over the San Francisco Giants.
“It was a lot of fun to watch tonight,” Rushing said. “Looked like himself.”
After three suboptimal innings, Glasnow settled down in a trust-building exercise of an outing against the Giants and their triple A-caliber lineup.
He wasn’t the most efficient, the most pristine, the sharpest — but he was fit to throw 98 pitches and six innings.
To fight through after laboring with 59 pitches in the first three innings, to earn his second win since April and to help the Dodgers maintain their four-game buffer over the Atlanta Braves as they play to secure a first-round bye with eight games left.
There was no champagne hangover for Glasnow on Friday — he flew directly back to L.A. from Miami, skipping Thursday’s clubhouse party in Cincinnati, where the Dodgers celebrated clinching the National League West Division for the 13th time in 14 years — but how about a toast to good health?
Cheers to giving up just two runs, one each in the second and third innings. To walking only two batters and striking out 10. To giving up only three hard hits and producing 15 whiffs.
To feeling and pitching better.
“After that third inning, I just stopped trying to be quick,” Glasnow said. “Just go out and be athletic, and I think it started to feel a little bit more timed up.”
Glasnow came into Friday’s game — one of his final two regular-season starts — having given up eight runs on 11 hits and seven walks in his previous two starts, looking less than comfortable in both. Out of rhythm, out of sync.
“This is an important start, and he knows it,” manager Dave Roberts said before the game. “It’s certainly not do or die, but ... just to kind of get back feeling good.”
Afterward, Roberts wasn’t thrilled with how Glasnow started, but liked how he finished.
“You could see him fighting himself a little bit,” Roberts said. “The fastball command wasn’t great early. Got a lot of strikeouts. Curveball wasn’t sharp. But I thought he did a good job of making pitches when he needed to. The slider got better, fastball command got better as the game went on. Good to see him get through six innings.”
It’ll be better yet for the Dodgers’ odds if Glasnow can carry Friday’s progress into his next start — and then into the playoffs, where he proved himself as a Dodger last season after an elbow sprain sidelined him for the 2024 postseason.
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
In the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series run, Glasnow made six appearances, three of them starts. He had a 1.69 ERA and averaged 10.5 strikeouts per nine innings. The stuff of aces.
“Today was a step in the right direction,” said Glasnow, the formerHart High School star, before leaving the clubhouse in flip-flops. “I’d rather kind of feel it, work through some stuff, and have a good one right before playoffs.
“I think I’m in a good spot right now.”

A week ago, Tyler Glasnow was beginning to turn back into a question mark.
So, the Dodgers sent him home and hoped he would reset.
Last Saturday, the All-Star pitcher looked all out of sorts in a four-inning, four-run and frankly foreboding start during the team’s visit to Miami.
He was battling his mechanics. He was stretching out his long-bothersome back. And, most concerningly, he was losing the confident demeanor the Dodgers had seen when he first returned from his latest extended stint on the injured list last month.
Thus, instead of accompanying the team on the second leg of its road trip this week in Cincinnati, Glasnow traveled immediately back to Los Angeles the day after his clunker against the Marlins.
No extra flight. No added time on the road. Just a week where he could focus on his delivery and try to keep his season from once again slipping off track.
“He got back on Pacific Standard Time, in his own bed, one leg of travel versus the two,” manager Dave Roberts said Friday afternoon. “He threw his bullpen a few days ago. That went great. So he’s dialed in.”
In a six-inning, two-run, 10-strikeout start in Friday’s 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants, there was still more dialing in left for Glasnow to do.
He hung a curveball in the second inning that Jung Hoo Lee belted for a home run.
He lost his feel pitching from the stretch after a leadoff single in the third, giving up another run that briefly put the Dodgers behind before they stormed back with five home runs –– including four in the eighth inning alone –– from their recently resurgent offense.
The important thing, though, was that Glasnow felt better.
With his health. With his throw. With his ability to get completely synced up in time for the playoffs.
“I think I feel relatively consistent. It’s just a matter of, sometimes I’m not going to feel good, sometimes I will,” Glasnow said. “Today, I think it was a step in the right direction. I think it’s better than feeling really good for a long time before [the playoffs]. I’d rather kind of feel it, work through some stuff and have a good one right before playoffs. So I think I’m in a good spot right now.”
That might sound counter-intuitive for a pitcher who could be crucial to the Dodgers’ postseason plans. It might be rationalization from an 11-year veteran who has never made it through a full regular season healthy.
Then again, it’s a blueprint that worked well enough for Glasnow last year, when he only felt his mechanics click in the last few weeks before the start of the playoffs yet went on to post a 1.69 ERA in six October outings.
“It is just making sure he’s feeling good, he’s healthy, which he is,” Roberts said. “So now it’s just letting him go do what he does and bet on the talent to perform. That’s where I think we all feel good, especially Tyler right now, just knowing the health and where the head’s at, all that stuff. We’re in a good spot.”
Roberts struck a decidedly different tone after Glasnow’s start last week, saying then that the right-hander “didn’t feel great coming into the game as far as kind of overall body.”
That revelation raised alarm bells regarding the oft-injured 33-year-old –– who had already missed more than three months this season with a back spasms problem that lasted far longer than initially anticipated.
His absence in Cincinnati was also conspicuous, turning Friday’s outing into something of a late-season litmus test.
“This is an important start,” Roberts said beforehand. “He knows it.”
The manager’s evaluation afterward?
“I thought he did a good job of making pitches when he needed to,” Roberts said, encouraged by Glasnow’s ability to get swing-and-miss, as well as the way he retired 10 of his final 11 batters in a 98-pitch performance.
For his part, Glasnow downplayed whatever concerns had been lingering about his health of late.
He acknowledged he felt “not great” last week. He cited the cross-country flight as perhaps getting him out of whack. But he also noted that, “in the course of a season, you’re not always going to feel good.”
“It wasn’t anything crazy,” he added. “But I definitely feel better now than I did then.”
At this point, that will have to be enough for the Dodgers. Come the start of the postseason, they will be counting on him to be an effective member of their rotation.
“Right now, I feel pretty good,” Glasnow said. “We worked on some stuff after that last start. Just tried to keep for this start, take it in the next start. And then hopefully everything is feeling good for playoffs.”

LOS ANGELES — There was no hangover at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium.
Not after clinching the National League West. Not with the champagne still fresh in the Dodgers’ minds. And certainly not with Josue De Paula getting his first real taste of the big stage in Chavez Ravine.
Instead, the Dodgers looked very much like a team preparing for October. And De Paula looked like a player who wants to be part of it.
The 21-year-old came through with the go-ahead RBI double in the sixth inning Friday night, turning a tie game into a Dodgers lead and helping spark what eventually became an 8-2 victory over the Giants.
“It felt amazing,” De Paula said. “To do that for the team, give us the lead. I’m just celebrating with the boys. I just want to see us win.”
That last part might have been the most telling.
De Paula isn't approaching his first week in the major leagues like a player trying to prove he belongs with a franchise full of veterans and established stars. At least publicly, he's approaching it like a kid soaking in every moment.
But his performance is making it increasingly difficult for the Dodgers to ignore what he might bring when the calendar flips to October.
Dave Roberts acknowledged as much after the game.
“He’s certainly doing a lot of things well,” Roberts said when asked about De Paula potentially being part of the Dodgers’ postseason roster mix.
For now, De Paula says he's trying not to look too far ahead.
“Yeah, it’s crossed my mind,” he said of making the postseason roster. “Like I said, I try to focus on the now, right here. I’m enjoying every moment with these veteran players.”
The now, on Friday, was pretty impressive.
De Paula came to the plate in the fifth inning with the Dodgers trailing 2-1 and opened the frame with a single, his first hit at Dodger Stadium.
Mookie Betts followed with a single of his own, and Teoscar Hernández brought De Paula home with an RBI single to tie the game.
One inning later, De Paula was back in the middle of it.
This time, he delivered the biggest swing of the night to that point, lining an RBI double to put the Dodgers ahead.
A player who had spent years dreaming about moments like this had just created one.
“It was awesome,” De Paula said of his first week in the majors. “Like I said, everybody, the manager, all the teammates have been amazing and accepting me.”
There is, however, one part of his game De Paula knows still needs work.
His defense. And he's not shying away from it.
“I know that's a big area and improvement for me,” De Paula said. “I know I got a lot of hate on it. So I'm that type: if I get hate on it, I'm gonna focus on it more. So I'm gonna shut a lot of people up with my defense very soon.”
That confidence is unmistakable.
So is the willingness to accept criticism and use it as motivation.
The Dodgers don't need De Paula to become a finished product overnight. They need to determine whether his offensive impact, approach and overall upside give them enough reason to keep him around as they prepare for a postseason run.
And his teammates are already noticing what he does at the plate.
Betts, who knows something about making an impression in a Dodgers uniform, spoke highly of De Paula's at-bats.
“He's swinging at strikes, taking balls, impacting the ball,” Betts said. “There's no matchup that is really a bad matchup, which is really neat to see someone so young that can handle it…. He's been awesome.”
That might be the most encouraging part of De Paula's arrival.
The results are one thing. The at-bats are another.
He's not simply getting by on raw talent. He's showing an ability to recognize strikes, lay off pitches outside the zone and impact the baseball against major-league pitching.
And on a night when the Dodgers needed a spark, he provided it.
Of course, De Paula wasn't the only Dodger putting on a show.
Betts got the night started with a leadoff home run in the first inning, crushing the second pitch he saw from Giants left-hander Cesar Perdomo, a 93 mph fastball, into the left-field pavilion.
It was the 33rd leadoff home run of Betts' career.
Later, after the Giants briefly took control, Betts came back with another home run in the eighth inning, his second of the night and his 22nd of the season.
That's two more home runs than he hit last season, with eight games remaining.
Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker then went back-to-back, before Will Smith joined the party.
Four Dodgers, Muncy, Tucker, Betts and Smith, homered in the eighth inning.
What began as a competitive game suddenly became a rout. Muncy's home run gave him 29 for the season, while Tucker continued to show signs of heating up at precisely the time the Dodgers want their lineup clicking.
But none of that changes what made Friday night particularly interesting.
The Dodgers already know what Betts, Muncy, Tucker and Smith can do. They are still learning what De Paula can become.
And on his first night in the big-league spotlight at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium, he gave them another reason to keep watching.
Tyler Glasnow did his part, too.
After Betts gave the Dodgers an early 1-0 lead, Glasnow surrendered a solo home run to Jung Hoo Lee in the second inning before Jonah Cox's RBI single put San Francisco ahead in the third.
From there, Glasnow settled down.
He finished with six innings, allowing three hits and two runs while walking two and striking out 10 on 98 pitches, 63 of them for strikes.
The bullpen took it from there, while the Dodgers' offense eventually turned a close game into another comfortable victory.
They are now 94-60 on the season and remain two games behind Milwaukee for the top seed in the National League, while building a four-game cushion over Atlanta for third place.
The division has already been won. The real work is beginning now.
De Paula says he's focused on the present.
The Dodgers, meanwhile, have to be thinking about the future.
Because if Friday was any indication, Josue De Paula isn't simply here to experience the major leagues.
He's here to make it increasingly difficult to send him anywhere else.
